newsitem.title: USA: White House sees budget deal with Congress in spring.
newsitem.headline: White House sees budget deal with Congress in spring.

text.p: The White House hopes to reach a deal with Congress this spring to balance the budget and wipe out the deficit by 2002, the budget director for the Clinton administration said on Wednesday.

"I hope we have a budget deal this spring," Office of Management and Budget Director Franklin Raines said. Actual implementation of any budget deal would likely occur after Congress' August recess, he added.

"I hope we have a budget deal as soon as possible and I think if we were to work hard we could have a budget deal in time for the congressional budget resolution adoption. That process gets kicked off around the middle of April," Raines said after testifying at a congressional hearing.

The budget resolution maps out the spending and tax targets for the coming fiscal year that starts Oct. 1, and is not signed by the president. Separate legislation must be passed and signed by Clinton to implement decisions made in the budget process.
Raines expected a deal to be reached despite the fact that negotiations were not in full swing yet and spring is only weeks away. "This is the normal gestation process," he said.

House Majority Leader Dick Armey of Texas said he believed the budget process would be less confrontational this time around. In the last Congress, fights over the budget forced two government shutdowns.
"So far, as the budget is more acceptable to the president, the reconciliation bills can be more acceptable and we won't find ourselves in a mess at the end of the year," Armey said.

"We will produce our own budget but it is not going to be a 'face-off' budget," meaning that during the process there would be comprehensive consultations within Congress and with the administration, he said.

Raines acknowledged that reaching agreement would not be easy, and said sticking points included a $50 billion difference over what the deficit would be in 2002 and also the magnitude of tax proposals.
Meanwhile, a coalition of 22 moderate-to-conservative Democrats released their own proposal which they said would balance the budget by 2002 and did not include any tax cuts.
The group known as the "Blue Dog" Democrats also jumped into an area that others have skirted by proposing a reduction in cost of living increases tied to the consumer price index.
The coalition proposed a downward adjustment of 0.8 percent because the CPI is estimated to overstate inflation by 1.1 percent.
The coalition said its plan would achieve $103.7 billion in savings over five years from the CPI-related adjustment.
Republicans have said they want President Clinton to take the lead on any CPI-related changes. Programmes linked to the measure include Social Security and veterans benefits.
